title: Running Through Ramadan: A Practical Guide for Muslim Runners in Southeast Asia
seo_title: Running Through Ramadan: A Guide for SEA Muslim Runners
meta_description: When to train, how much to drink and what to eat while fasting, what the research on fasting runners shows, and how many races in our calendar fall in Ramadan 2027, by country.
dek: Fasting reshapes a full month of training every year for a large share of the region's runners. What sports-nutrition guidance says about doing it well, and what Ramadan 2027 looks like on the race calendar.

sections.heading: Ramadan 2027 on the Race Calendar
paragraphs: Ramadan 1448 is expected to run from about 8 February to 9 March 2027. Indonesia's Muhammadiyah, which sets its dates by calculation, has fixed 1 Ramadan on Monday 8 February 2027 [4]. Singapore's Ministry of Manpower lists Hari Raya Puasa as Wednesday 10 March 2027 [5], and Indonesia's joint ministerial holiday calendar puts Idul Fitri on 10 and 11 March [6]. Other authorities confirm their dates by sighting the new moon, so the first or last day can differ by one day from country to country [6].

Our calendar lists 11 races between 8 February and 9 March 2027: seven in Thailand and one each in the Philippines, Vietnam, Myanmar and Laos. None are in Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore or Brunei [7]. The gap is sharp. Malaysia has 12 races listed for January 2027 and none again until the Miri Marathon on 21 March. In Indonesia, the Sanur Bali International Half Marathon runs on 7 February, the day before Ramadan is expected to start, and the next listed race is the Carabao Half Marathon on 28 March [7].

Two caveats. The early-2027 calendar is still filling up, because many organisers announce dates only a few months ahead. And the count covers races we list, not every event. Even so, the pattern fits what runners in Muslim-majority countries see each year: organisers tend to leave the fasting month clear and pack races into the weeks either side. For a Muslim runner, the realistic fasting-month races are mostly abroad, which is worth knowing before entering one.

sections.heading: What Fasting Does, and Doesn't Do, to Running
paragraphs: The most direct evidence comes from a study of 15 trained male distance runners who fasted through Ramadan. Their calorie, carbohydrate and water intake fell, and so did their daily training time. Yet by the last week of Ramadan their time to exhaustion and top running speed on a treadmill test had improved slightly, with maximal oxygen uptake unchanged [3]. The authors conclude that, with training adjusted sensibly, distance runners can maintain or even slightly improve performance through the month [3].

The important qualifier is that these runners cut their training. The finding supports a lighter, well-managed month, not training as usual while fasting. Sports dietitians make the same point: the runners who struggle are usually the ones who try to keep their normal volume, intensity and timing [1][2].

sections.heading: Choosing When to Train
paragraphs: The Malaysian Dietitians' Association sets out three windows, each with a trade-off [1]. A morning session after sunrise benefits from the meals the night before and before dawn, but leaves little chance to refuel, rehydrate and recover until evening. A session finishing just before iftar is done on minimal support, but recovery food comes straight after. A session two to three hours after breaking the fast gives the best chance to fuel and hydrate, but has to be balanced against sleep.

The association suggests putting heavy sessions in the early evening after breaking the fast, and keeping light or technical training at the usual time [1]. The British Dietetic Association similarly suggests moving high-intensity sessions closer to iftar where possible, so food and fluid follow quickly [2]. In a region where many runners already train before dawn, the simplest change is to keep easy runs in the morning, short and slow, and move the long run and the hard session to the evening.

Heat matters more than usual. The Malaysian dietitians advise that an athlete who is down 3% or more of usual body weight from dehydration should not do strenuous, prolonged exercise, especially in the heat [1]. Weighing yourself before training for a few days is a cheap way to catch a creeping deficit.

sections.heading: Drinking and Eating Across the Non-Fasting Hours
paragraphs: The British Dietetic Association suggests about 2 to 3 litres of fluid spread across the hours between iftar and suhoor, taken steadily rather than in large amounts at once, which mostly end up as urine. It also warns that a lot of caffeine adds to fluid and salt losses, and suggests adding salt in cooking rather than at the table, since extra salt can increase thirst [2].

For suhoor, both associations advise eating as close to dawn as possible and choosing slow-release carbohydrate and protein [1][2]. The Malaysian dietitians give rice with egg, cheese and milk as examples [1]. Iftar traditionally opens with dates and water, a quick source of sugar and fluid, followed by a full meal with carbohydrate, protein and vegetables that also covers recovery on training days. Sodium and fluid guidance for long, hot runs is covered at runsea.run/articles/electrolytes-and-sodium-beyond-just-water-in-the-heat/.

sections.heading: When a Race Falls During Ramadan
paragraphs: Treat the month as maintenance, not a time to chase a personal best. A race abroad during Ramadan is best run on a conservative pace plan, with extra fluid and carbohydrate at suhoor and in the days before. The fast begins at dawn, well before sunrise, so whether you finish before it starts depends on the flag-off time, your pace and the local dawn time. A very early half-marathon start may leave enough time; a marathon generally will not. Check the start time and cut-off against the local dawn time before entering, and plan to run any fasting part easy.

Fasting is not required of everyone. The British Dietetic Association notes that people who are ill, pregnant, elderly or children can seek exemption, and that people with diabetes should get medical advice before fasting [2]. Whether to race while fasting is a personal and religious decision. None of this replaces advice from a doctor or a religious authority.

faqs.question: When is Ramadan 2027?
faqs.answer: Ramadan 1448 is expected to run from about 8 February to 9 March 2027. Muhammadiyah has set 1 Ramadan on 8 February, and Singapore and Indonesia list Hari Raya Puasa or Idul Fitri on 10 March. Authorities that use moon sighting confirm their dates closer to the time, so they can differ by a day.

faqs.question: Are there races in Malaysia or Indonesia during Ramadan 2027?
faqs.answer: None in our calendar so far. Of the 11 races we list between 8 February and 9 March 2027, seven are in Thailand and one each in the Philippines, Vietnam, Myanmar and Laos. Malaysia's listings stop after January and resume on 21 March. Some organisers have not yet announced early-2027 dates.

faqs.question: What's the best time to train during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Dietitians suggest putting hard or long sessions in the early evening after breaking the fast, or finishing them just before iftar, so food and fluid follow quickly. Easy morning runs work if they are short, since there is no chance to refuel until evening.

faqs.question: How much should a runner drink during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: The British Dietetic Association suggests about 2 to 3 litres spread across the non-fasting hours, sipped steadily rather than drunk in large amounts at once, and going easy on caffeine.
